segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: A quick warning-- there are curse words that are unbeeped in this episode of the show. If you prefer a beeped version, you can find that at our website, thisamericanlife.org.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: So sure, over $11 billion is being spent on advertising for the election next week. But, of course, in addition to the ads, there are still human beings out there in this election trying to persuade the old-fashioned way-- person to person in one-on-one conversations, which is where you really see what people are made of and how they're deciding who they're going to vote for. People really say some stuff.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: One of our producers, Ike Sriskandarajah met this woman, Rose Johnson, in Detroit. The Senate race there is too close to call. And one problem that the Democrat Abdul El-Sayed's been having is getting Black voters. Rose has been out trying to convince those voters. And Ike, who is she?

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: OK, so Rose is a retired police dispatcher. She's a great-grandmother, and she's only been doing this about a year, but she's already worked on seven campaigns. She kind of got obsessed.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And you met at a community center?

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: Yeah. At the front of the room, her reverend was hosting this live radio show, and there's about 50 people who showed up to hear it. They're all Black. And the show spent about half an hour telling people to get out and vote for Abdul El-Sayed. But Rose didn't need the nudge. She was already on board.

segments.speaker: Rose Johnson
segments.text: I mean, he comes here all the time, so we see him all the time.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: She's done so many events that he's been at that now he actually knows her.

segments.speaker: Rose Johnson
segments.text: I stand behind him 1,000% because I feel comfortable with him. He's very, very approachable. He reaches out to you, and when you see him and you meet him, he knows you. So if he's in a crowd, he's going to wave at you. He's going to hug you if he can because he knows you. He don't act funny. He's the guy.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: She's knocked on doors for him. She's done phone banking, but she knows lots of people don't agree with her, even people who usually vote for Democrats.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: If he's showing up, like you're saying, why don't people like him?

segments.speaker: Rose Johnson
segments.text: It's just the religion. They want to say, oh, the Arab. I don't see that.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: Have people told that to you?

segments.speaker: Rose Johnson
segments.text: Yes. I have a friend of mine's, and she talks crazy anyway. And she said, well, I have to be honest with you, I can't vote for him because he's an Arab. And I said, well, that's dumb because they said the same thing about Kamala Harris. They said Kamala Harris, they wouldn't vote for her because she's a Black woman. So I get so upset when people say that. And if she wants to be my friend, she's going to do the right thing and vote for Abdul. Otherwise, I just can't mess with her. I don't want to hear her complaining about, oh, oh, oh. I don't want to hear it.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: And the things she's saying came up with basically every Black supporter of El-Sayed I talked to while I was in Detroit. They all describe this decades-long tension between Arabs who own stores and the Black patrons who shop there. Detroit has seen decades of violence, distrust, and racism between these two groups. And Rose has seen this attitude towards Arabs and other newcomers, too.

segments.speaker: Rose Johnson
segments.text: They get businesses. They get stores. They get loans. They get a lot of things that we didn't get coming into this country as African-Americans, and they just feel like they're entitled. Just don't come here and act like you're better than us, you're privileged. We get that enough from white people.

segments.speaker: Rose Johnson
segments.text: So we don't need that from others. We need to band against white people, you know, my opinion. Because it's us against them. That's my opinion.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: I mean, she says that with people she knows, she's been able to talk them out of their prejudice and into a vote for El-Sayed. But there's this one person in her life. You heard her talking about her earlier, one of her oldest friends, and she's been making the case to her for weeks. And I asked if I could listen in and record their conversation.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: --with your friend.

segments.speaker: Rose Johnson
segments.text: I can call her now.

segments.speaker: Rose Johnson
segments.text: [CHUCKLING]

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: She said yeah?

segments.speaker: Rose Johnson
segments.text: I'm going to put you on speaker.

segments.speaker: Cynthia
segments.text: OK.

segments.speaker: Rose Johnson
segments.text: So tell me your opinion of Abdul and why you-- are you going to vote for him?

segments.speaker: Cynthia
segments.text: No.

segments.speaker: Rose Johnson
segments.text: Why?

segments.speaker: Cynthia
segments.text: I don't want to.

segments.speaker: Rose Johnson
segments.text: I mean, can you elaborate?

segments.speaker: Cynthia
segments.text: I really can't say why I won't vote for that Abdul guy, because to be honest with you, I don't trust him. That's why I won't vote for him.

segments.speaker: Rose Johnson
segments.text: What is it about him you don't trust?

segments.speaker: Cynthia
segments.text: His nationality.

segments.speaker: Rose Johnson
segments.text: What does that have to do with anything?

segments.speaker: Cynthia
segments.text: A lot. What I'm saying is I want to vote for an American.

segments.speaker: Rose Johnson
segments.text: He is an American.

segments.speaker: Cynthia
segments.text: I want to keep it American.

segments.speaker: Rose Johnson
segments.text: He's Arabic American.

segments.speaker: Cynthia
segments.text: No, no, no, not in my book.

segments.speaker: Rose Johnson
segments.text: We're African-American.

segments.speaker: Cynthia
segments.text: That's different. I'll vote for them.

segments.speaker: Rose Johnson
segments.text: For us?

segments.speaker: Cynthia
segments.text: I'm not going to vote for him. I'm just being honest with you.

segments.speaker: Rose Johnson
segments.text: OK.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: Can I ask, is there anything he could change, like a policy, or is there anything he could say? By the way, this is-- my name is Ike. I'm a reporter talking to your friend Rose about El-Sayed, and I was wondering, is there an argument or something that you could hear that would change your mind?

segments.speaker: Cynthia
segments.text: There probably is, but it just-- I don't trust him. I'm not clear on none of his point of view. I haven't listened to none of his speeches.

segments.speaker: Rose Johnson
segments.text: So would you like to meet him in person, have a conversation with him? Because I can arrange that.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: This is one of Rose's special moves. It's kind of a flex. This is exactly how she got her sister to vote for Detroit's current mayor. She just put them on the phone together.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Oh, wow.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: But when Rose offered the same thing, like, Do you want to meet El-Sayed in person? she said no. She just can't right now. She said she's got too much going on. Her brother just passed away, and she's heading down to his funeral.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: So did Rose give up?

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: No. I mean, Rose is just as stubborn as her friend. And she said, I am going to take her to the polls. I'm going to hold her hand right up until the booth. And when she goes into the booth, the place that I can't go, I'm going to be whispering outside the booth-- Abdul, Abdul, Abdul.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Well, ladies and gentlemen, for all the talk the last few weeks about how so many people have changed their minds about President Trump and the Republicans, and all the talk about how tables are about to turn in these midterm elections, let us remember, please, how hard it is to change anybody's mind.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Today on our program, we have stories about people who are not changing their minds so easily and some unusual and extraordinary things being done to try to get them to change, including a tale of millions and millions of dollars being spent, all in the hope that just one person-- one person-- will change her mind. That's our first act today. From WBEZ Chicago, it's This American Life. I'm Ira Glass. Stay with us.

segments.speaker: Heather Tal Murphy
segments.text: Lots of things about Alani Bankhead's biography are perfect for someone running for Senate. She's former Air Force, 44 years old, counterterrorism specialist, intelligence analyst. Then she became a child sex crimes investigator. She's been part of dozens of convictions.

segments.speaker: Heather Tal Murphy
segments.text: She thought the Republican incumbent was doing a terrible job. He didn't show up for important votes. He didn't seem in touch with voters around the state. She was really bothered by that, and so she decided to run. She drafted up an announcement and posted it to social media, to LinkedIn.

segments.speaker: Heather Tal Murphy
segments.text: Why LinkedIn?

segments.speaker: Alani Bankhead
segments.text: I love LinkedIn. Yeah, LinkedIn is my jam.

segments.speaker: Heather Tal Murphy
segments.text: It's unconventional for a political announcement.

segments.speaker: Alani Bankhead
segments.text: Oh, well, I'm not a politician. I'm a public servant. I like to see myself that way anyway.

segments.speaker: Heather Tal Murphy
segments.text: She knew she was a long shot to win the race. In the Democratic primary, she was running against four other people, two far more established. She'd never, ever run for anything before, never been to a city council meeting or a protest.

segments.speaker: Heather Tal Murphy
segments.text: And she was still pretty new to Montana, moved here just a few years ago from Hawaii. She had few connections, no family ranch. Montana has also never sent a woman or a person of color to the Senate. Alani is both. She's Puerto Rican.

segments.speaker: Heather Tal Murphy
segments.text: It went about how you'd imagine. A few months after announcing, Alani found her campaign floundering. She'd raised less than $15,000, a tiny amount for a Senate campaign. All of her media was homemade, and her positions were boilerplate Democratic stuff-- affordability and the war in Iran, stop dark money in politics. She was getting very little attention, and then, one day in May, everything changed.

segments.speaker: Alani Bankhead
segments.text: I was in the car with my campaign manager. I don't remember where exactly. I think we were driving somewhere. And her stepdad had texted her, and he was like, I love the ad on TV. And we're like, what ad?

segments.speaker: Ad Narrator 1
segments.text: Democrat Alani Bankhead, US Air Force veteran running for Senate to fight for our public lands, for affordable health care, and to stand up to MAGA Republicans who think they're above the law. Alani Bankhead, the fighter we need in the US Senate.

segments.speaker: Heather Tal Murphy
segments.text: The ad was good-- slow-motion, gauzy shots of Alani, an old photo from her Air Force days looking veteran-y. And there were more ads, Alani walking with her police dog.

segments.speaker: Ad Narrator 2
segments.text: Alani Bankhead is stepping up to defend our public lands from the Trump agenda. Alani Bankhead, the proven fighter we need.

segments.speaker: Heather Tal Murphy
segments.text: And at that point, did you know who was creating them?

segments.speaker: Alani Bankhead
segments.text: No, had no idea. I remember running on the treadmill at the gym and seeing myself twice in a 20-minute run. And I was like, I need to get the hell out of here.

segments.speaker: Heather Tal Murphy
segments.text: On one hand, this was a huge gift falling out of the sky, but it was also confusing. Who was doing it?

segments.speaker: Alani Bankhead
segments.text: It felt really weird because I was skeptical. I'm like, why are these people putting these ads on? What do they want? Nobody had approached us. There had been zero conversations. We hadn't gotten a whiff of anything, so we didn't know what was happening.

segments.speaker: Heather Tal Murphy
segments.text: What were all the things that went through as possibilities for you?

segments.speaker: Alani Bankhead
segments.text: So it was either amazing angel investor or some nefarious plot. I was like, is someone trying to influence me later on in the election or some very-- like a MacKenzie Bezos, like, really generous person who was like, I see her and her background, and we need to help her.

segments.speaker: Heather Tal Murphy
segments.text: The TV ad blitz was accompanied by glossy mailers, social media ads, text messages, and phone calls. This kind of thing happens. Super PACs up and pay for ads for candidates who have no idea who they are. But this was an extreme version of it. Suddenly, this totally unknown novice's campaign had way more money pouring in on its behalf than anyone else in her race, 10 times more money than the obvious frontrunner, a former state lawmaker who'd been campaigning for two years.

segments.speaker: Heather Tal Murphy
segments.text: There was a name on these commercials, a super PAC called Progressive Vet PAC. Alani had never heard of it, but the name made sense. She's a veteran. FEC filings showed that the super PAC had raised $2.8 million, and it seemed to have been created specifically to support her.

segments.speaker: Heather Tal Murphy
segments.text: This kind of super PAC money is something Alani actively campaigns against, so she put out statements on social media saying, these are not our ads. Because this was a super PAC, and it's illegal for super PACs to coordinate with political candidates, Alani and her campaign didn't believe they could call them up and ask a lot of questions.

segments.speaker: Heather Tal Murphy
segments.text: On the PAC's financial documents, there were only two names-- someone who's listed as treasurer and a compliance guy. It's impossible to see who donated most of the money. But a few $100,000 were connected to a billionaire finance guy named Jason Carroll. Carroll co-founded a company that's involved in 10% of all the trades in the US stock market. The ads kept pouring in.

segments.speaker: Heather Tal Murphy
segments.text: On primary night in June, Alani and her husband held a watch party at a divey bar in the state capital, one where lobbyists and lawmakers often hang out. There were little American flags dangling from the ceiling. The huge influx of ads had taken Alani from an unknown to getting stopped by strangers at the grocery store and at the gas station.

segments.speaker: Heather Tal Murphy
segments.text: The ad blitz had been so sudden. There were no fresh polls to predict how the vote would shake out. Alani watched as the first results were tallied.

segments.speaker: Alani Bankhead
segments.text: As soon as that first chart hit the screen, I was at the top, and it didn't stop. And we won by double digits, so pretty decisive win. It was crazy. It was just-- I mean, you're just in shock, right? Because in January, everybody was like, who the hell is this girl? She's never going to win.

segments.speaker: Alani Bankhead
segments.text: [APPLAUSE]

segments.speaker: Heather Tal Murphy
segments.text: Alani Bankhead had essentially gone from political nobody to runaway US Senate nominee in just three weeks' time.

segments.speaker: Alani Bankhead
segments.text: And if tonight proves anything, it's this. Never underestimate what one person can do. The future of this country will not be decided by the loudest people online or the richest people in Washington. It will be decided by individuals.

segments.speaker: Heather Tal Murphy
segments.text: This, of course, is not what happened. It was the opposite. The loudest, richest people had completely turned this race upside down and propelled a totally unlikely candidate to a double-digit victory.

segments.speaker: Heather Tal Murphy
segments.text: After the primary, rumors start flying about who had just elevated Alani Bankhead from long-shot unknown to the Democratic nominee for Senate in just weeks. Who was behind this giant infusion of super PAC money?

segments.speaker: Heather Tal Murphy
segments.text: And I'll get to that mystery in a minute, but for any of this to make any sense to you, I need to explain how the race laid out at this point.

segments.speaker: Heather Tal Murphy
segments.text: Alani was now set up to face a Republican, former US attorney named Kurt Alme, a Trump loyalist who'd been lined up by the outgoing Republican senator. She was also-- and this is important-- facing a second candidate, an independent named Seth Bodnar. His ads were running everywhere.

segments.speaker: Seth Bodnar
segments.text: In Washington, they force you into a box-- Democrat or Republican-- and you vote how you're told to, even if it hurts your state. I reject that.

segments.speaker: Heather Tal Murphy
segments.text: Bodnar, like Alani, is former military-- served in Iraq, a Green Beret.

segments.speaker: Seth Bodnar
segments.text: I'm not a politician. I'm a soldier, a businessman, a husband, a father.

segments.speaker: Heather Tal Murphy
segments.text: Bodnar's resume is full of impressive credentials-- first in his class at West Point, two master's degrees from Oxford, Rhodes Scholar, a Bronze Star. And unlike Alani Bankhead, Bodnar has deeper ties and way more political connections in Montana. His wife's a fifth generation Montanan. His most recent job-- president of the University of Montana, which, of course, brings all kinds of personal and political connections across the state. A perfect centrist candidate for this political moment.

segments.speaker: Heather Tal Murphy
segments.text: So that's what Alani was up against. But she looked at this formidable opponent and thought, well, OK, this is the part where Montana Democrats will unite behind their nominee. Instead, something strange happened. Those millions of dollars of mysterious ads supporting her stopped running. Alani started getting calls from reporters about the Progressive Vet PAC that had funded those ads.

segments.speaker: Alani Bankhead
segments.text: They're, like, Progressive Vet PAC is saying your race is unviable or something about you can't win. So we're taking our money elsewhere. And I was, like, bye. I mean, we didn't ask for that money anyway. And that's what we told all the reporters, right? We're, like, we didn't ask for this money. We don't want dark money. We're opposed to dark money.

segments.speaker: Heather Tal Murphy
segments.text: In other words, the group that put her on the map was abandoning her. So what was going on here? Well, Montana is one of five red states where Democrats are so unpopular, the brand is so toxic, that lots of Democrats have concluded that in certain races that no Democrat can win. So the best path to victory is to back an independent.

segments.speaker: Heather Tal Murphy
segments.text: And in four of those states-- Idaho, Nebraska, South Dakota and Alaska-- they did it. The Democratic nominee bowed out over the summer, leaving the field open for independent candidates in those states to sweep up all the voters who are unhappy with Trump and the Republicans. This is what so many of us in Montana thought was happening here.

segments.speaker: Heather Tal Murphy
segments.text: The rumor was Democratic strategists threw themselves behind the independent, Seth Bodnar, hoping they could get the Democratic nominee to drop out. And to ensure that it happened, they took an extra step during the primary. They urged their rich donors to send money to the newcomer, Alani Bankhead, figuring as a newbie she'd be the most likely to drop out. Anyway, that was the rumor. And that was what Alani suspected.

segments.speaker: Heather Tal Murphy
segments.text: Something that looked fishy to Alani was that the billionaire connected to the Super PAC, Jason Carroll, had also given money to Bodnar.

segments.speaker: Alani Bankhead
segments.text: So to me, that's as much of a smoking gun as you're going to get to show that Progressive Vet PAC was pro Bodnar. I think with the intent of get Alani elected and get Alani pushed out of the election.

segments.speaker: Heather Tal Murphy
segments.text: So it reaffirmed that it was a nefarious plot?

segments.speaker: Alani Bankhead
segments.text: Yes, it did.

segments.speaker: Heather Tal Murphy
segments.text: Why do you think you were misread as someone who was more likely to drop out, or the most likely to drop out?

segments.speaker: Alani Bankhead
segments.text: I think because I'm female, and I look really young, and I'm Brown, and I'm petite, and I'm kind. And people have mistooken that for weakness my entire career. She's cute and adorable. She's a pushover. Like, she won't be that hard, which I think is really hilarious because jokes on them. Eat shit. Get some better consultants.

segments.speaker: Heather Tal Murphy
segments.text: I reached out to Carroll the billionaire, but he didn't respond. I also tried to get the Super PAC's treasurer. When I asked Seth Bodnar about what happened in the Democratic primary, he said flat out he was not part of any plan to force out any Democratic nominee. He wasn't involved. Doesn't know where the money came from that poured into Alani's campaign.

segments.speaker: Heather Tal Murphy
segments.text: So where did the money come from? Who was behind it? Who had just elevated Alani Bankhead from long shot unknown to the Democratic nominee and then hung her out to dry? I called all kinds of people about this, Democratic insiders and operatives. No one was exactly sure what had happened or if the rumors were true until I got to Max Baucus. Baucus is a huge deal for Montana Democrats. He was a Democratic Senator here for more than three decades. He knows everyone.

segments.speaker: Max Baucus
segments.text: No, I was not, but I do know of some people who were involved.

segments.speaker: Heather Tal Murphy
segments.text: Who was involved?

segments.speaker: Max Baucus
segments.text: Some people I know involved in Montana campaigns, really wonderful people. They were part of some organizations that directed the money. It was a mistake.

segments.speaker: Heather Tal Murphy
segments.text: But they told you that they were going to pick somebody who would be more likely to withdraw? Somebody told you that?

segments.speaker: Max Baucus
segments.text: Yes, that's correct.

segments.speaker: Heather Tal Murphy
segments.text: OK.

segments.speaker: Max Baucus
segments.text: That's correct.

segments.speaker: Heather Tal Murphy
segments.text: Baucus wouldn't name names, but he's one of many big name Democrats in Montana who've thrown all their support behind Bodnar, the independent candidate, saying he's their best shot at beating the Republican and going on at length about what an amazing, impressive person Bodnar is. Since that conversation, I've spoken with politicians and political insiders, and as best as I can reconstruct, here's what happened.

segments.speaker: Heather Tal Murphy
segments.text: It all began with a meeting in August 2025 in Anaconda with Democratic politicians and strategists from Montana and beyond. They talked about how only an independent could win certain races in the State, and their win would require getting the Democrat to withdraw. Meanwhile, Bodnar, this promising former Green Beret who some Democrats had been eyeing for years, decided he was ready to take the plunge as an independent.

segments.speaker: Heather Tal Murphy
segments.text: One Democratic insider told me about later conversations, where strategists discussed which Democratic candidate would be the best to push out after the primary. There was the Native American man. They decided it would look bad to push him out. And they knew the front runner, the former state lawmaker, would never drop out. She'd said so many times. So they settled on Alani Bankhead, though no one spoke to her about this.

segments.speaker: Heather Tal Murphy
segments.text: In Nebraska, where Democrats were also running this strategy, they did get a commitment from the Democratic nominee to drop out in advance. Democrats didn't make an agreement like that with Alani, but they funded her during the primary because they needed someone to knock the front-runner out of the race. And if you talk to the front-runner about what happened, that is definitely how she sees it. Her name is Reilly Neill.

segments.speaker: Reilly Neill
segments.text: It was a purposeful effort to repress my race. And I can't say that after this experience, I feel like much of a Democrat.

segments.speaker: Heather Tal Murphy
segments.text: She told me about this one very unsettling phone call she says she got right before Bodnar entered the race from a well-known Democrat in the state.

segments.speaker: Reilly Neill
segments.text: And he said, so how much would it take you to drop out of the race? $500,000? And I said, no. Hell no. I don't need that kind of money. I have plenty of money. And he's like, how about $15 million?

segments.speaker: Heather Tal Murphy
segments.text: No, he didn't.

segments.speaker: Reilly Neill
segments.text: And I said-- yes, he did. And I said--

segments.speaker: Heather Tal Murphy
segments.text: Where would he even get $15 million?

segments.speaker: Reilly Neill
segments.text: I laughed to make it less serious and said, how about $50 million? And I'm not dropping out. And then he laughed, and we ended the conversation.

segments.speaker: Heather Tal Murphy
segments.text: Did he say why he would want you to drop out?

segments.speaker: Reilly Neill
segments.text: No. I don't know if he was just-- it was a trial balloon or if it was sincere. I don't know. He could probably say I was just messing around. But you can ask my husband because I thought he was dead serious.

segments.speaker: Brian Schweitzer
segments.text: Oh, that's completely false.

segments.speaker: Heather Tal Murphy
segments.text: The person who she said made this offer to her? Former Montana Governor Brian Schweitzer, a Democrat. If the offer were sincere, this would break state law. I called up Schweitzer and told him what Reilly Neill said.

segments.speaker: Brian Schweitzer
segments.text: I have absolutely no idea about that.

segments.speaker: Brian Schweitzer
segments.text: [LAUGHS]

segments.speaker: Brian Schweitzer
segments.text: By the way, not only no idea, this is outrageous for her to have said that.

segments.speaker: Heather Tal Murphy
segments.text: OK. So she said that then the conversation switched, and she was quite surprised. And then you both laughed, and then you hung up, and then you didn't talk to her again for a while.

segments.speaker: Brian Schweitzer
segments.text: I may well have done that because the rumors were out there that people were getting offered to get out of the race.

segments.speaker: Heather Tal Murphy
segments.text: Wait, so what do you mean you may well have done that?

segments.speaker: Brian Schweitzer
segments.text: The rumors were all over the place that whoever won this race might be getting out of the race.

segments.speaker: Heather Tal Murphy
segments.text: I see. So you--

segments.speaker: Brian Schweitzer
segments.text: But I was not proposing anything to anybody. I was saying how ridiculous it would be that somebody would propose to pay money to get out of the race. I may have been making a point that you can't be bought. Maybe somebody else in this race can be bought. But I knew she couldn't be.

segments.speaker: Heather Tal Murphy
segments.text: He told me this whole story makes no sense. He endorsed Reilly Neill through the primary, then endorsed Alani after she won. He believes it's important for the party to stand behind their Democratic nominee.

segments.speaker: Heather Tal Murphy
segments.text: So after speaking with several people who've worked for Schweitzer, I don't think he was offering her a bribe. I think what might have been happening here is that he might have been trying to figure out if anyone could get Neill to drop out. So he threw these numbers at her, or he might have been making a joke. Who knows? Everyone's so paranoid at this point in Montana politics.

segments.speaker: Heather Tal Murphy
segments.text: Anyway, back to Alani. After the primary, this intense pressure campaign started to get her to drop out. Lawn signs started appearing all over the capital city of Helena.

segments.speaker: Alani Bankhead
segments.text: They papered Helena and my neighborhood with yard signs that said, "Alani drop out." We heard about that because one of our neighbors, he travels a lot for business. And as he was leaving at 4:00 AM, he called my husband and was like, hey, there are these signs around the neighborhood. We might have one. Do you want me to go get it?

segments.speaker: Heather Tal Murphy
segments.text: A yard sign?

segments.speaker: Alani Bankhead
segments.text: I think we might.

segments.speaker: Heather Tal Murphy
segments.text: She carried this big blue sign into her living room.

segments.speaker: Alani Bankhead
segments.text: So it says, Bow out Bankhead. Thank you, Alani. Please bow out. Paid for by Montana Freedom PAC. MTFreedomPAC.org. Not authorized by any candidate." The other side says, "Bow out Bankhead. Step back so Montana can step forward. Paid for by Montana Freedom PAC."

segments.speaker: Heather Tal Murphy
segments.text: The Montana Freedom PAC supports Bodnar. At this point, I have to pause and say whoever was in on the plans to boost Alani Bankhead with the idea that she'd be a pushover, that she would wither and quit, their scheming could have benefited from some more basic research about who she is. There's the frequently cited stuff, like working as a senior bodyguard for a secretary in the Air Force. But she's also a life coach and podcaster.

segments.speaker: Heather Tal Murphy
segments.text: People often point to her self-help podcast and sort of make fun of it for its live, laugh, love vibes. It's called Humble Warrior.

segments.speaker: Alani Bankhead
segments.text: Journey beyond imposter syndrome. This is where I invite you into a space where high achievers and spiritual leaders converge to redefine success and self-worth.

segments.speaker: Heather Tal Murphy
segments.text: But if you listen to what she's actually saying on it, her thing is, here's how to get past these moments when you feel like you're not qualified. Her whole focus is on telling people not to give up. She's written a book on it, runs trainings on this kind of thing for law enforcement. Still, the pressure on Alani has only increased and it's easy to see why.

segments.speaker: Heather Tal Murphy
segments.text: If the polls are right and nothing changes, the Republicans will easily hold on to Montana's Senate seat. The Republican is pulling over 40. Bodnar's numbers are in the high 20s or low 30s. And Alani is trailing behind them both in the teens. If she quit the race and Bodnar somehow picked up all her votes, he might win.

segments.speaker: Heather Tal Murphy
segments.text: She hasn't raised very much money since the primaries. Well, Bodnar has raised millions. Everyone in politics is seeing this, and Alani started to get calls from Democrats outside the state. They weren't actually telling her to drop out. It was more like, hey, looks like you don't have much of a chance. You have no money. How can you actually compete here?

segments.speaker: Heather Tal Murphy
segments.text: I heard that one of the calls was from one of Alani's political idols, Elissa Slotkin, a Democratic senator from Michigan also with a military background like her.

segments.speaker: Heather Tal Murphy
segments.text: So am I correct that-- did Elissa Slotkin call you and ask you to resign?

segments.speaker: Alani Bankhead
segments.text: I cannot confirm nor deny.

segments.speaker: Heather Tal Murphy
segments.text: Why not? Come on.

segments.speaker: Alani Bankhead
segments.text: Because that's not my style to name drop in that way.

segments.speaker: Heather Tal Murphy
segments.text: OK.

segments.speaker: Alani Bankhead
segments.text: I respect her.

segments.speaker: Heather Tal Murphy
segments.text: I reached out to Slotkin and didn't hear back.

segments.speaker: Alani Bankhead
segments.text: I mean, on the record, I had a US senator, a sitting governor, and a former member of cabinet call me to try to get me to drop out.

segments.speaker: Heather Tal Murphy
segments.text: Did any of them come visit you in person or all phone calls?

segments.speaker: Alani Bankhead
segments.text: One of them tried to come visit me in person, and I told them not to come because I just thought it was weird. And I suspected they were going to try to get me to drop out. And I was like, I don't want you to travel all this way for you to fail at your mission.

segments.speaker: Heather Tal Murphy
segments.text: So can I ask you, too, when these people called, did anyone ever offer you or hint at anything you would get? Like, we would support you in future runs, or maybe you could have a job, or we're going to support you?

segments.speaker: Alani Bankhead
segments.text: Oh, yes.

segments.speaker: Heather Tal Murphy
segments.text: What were kind of things that they tried to offer?

segments.speaker: Alani Bankhead
segments.text: Oh, yeah. There was probing. They were like what do you want to do next? And I was like, what do you mean? They're like, well, me and my colleagues, we got into the House and then I got into Senate and others are governors. Like, what's the next things?

segments.speaker: Alani Bankhead
segments.text: And I was like, nothing. I'm running for Senate, and that's it. And they're like, OK. And then they're like, the DNC is standing up this, like, female veteran, like, office to support female veterans running as Dems. Like, would you want to run it? And I was like, why would I go work for the same organization that has stabbed me in the back and told me that I'm not supportable? That makes no sense.

segments.speaker: Heather Tal Murphy
segments.text: Alani would not tell me who talked to her about this job and said they didn't explicitly ask her to drop out. But the state's Republican attorney general recently announced he's investigating what happened and whether it broke the law. The DNC says they never offered her a job.

segments.speaker: Heather Tal Murphy
segments.text: As Alani heads into the final days of the race, she says she hasn't had a moment of doubt about what she should do.

segments.speaker: Heather Tal Murphy
segments.text: There's no one out there, not on your campaign, who believes that you can win based on the polling numbers. Do you still think you could win?

segments.speaker: Alani Bankhead
segments.text: If polls mattered, Hillary would have won.

segments.speaker: Heather Tal Murphy
segments.text: She says if the Republican wins, she'll feel fine.

segments.speaker: Alani Bankhead
segments.text: I will be proud to have run the race that we did. And I mean, it will have been the people of Montana that voted that way. It's the people's choice. It's not my choice.

segments.speaker: Heather Tal Murphy
segments.text: Her response is always like this. She ran. She won the party's nomination. She didn't break any rules. If someone trying to manipulate the race is disappointed, that is their problem. It's like one part moral high ground, one part middle finger. The deadline for Alani to withdraw, for her name in the Democratic Party to be removed from the ballot, came and went. People are still urging her to suspend her campaign.

segments.speaker: Heather Tal Murphy
segments.text: Alani Bankhead's refusal to leave the race fueled a whole second pool of rumors. The rumors are that she's actually a tool of the Republicans, a Republican plant who's trying to split the anti-Trump vote to help the Republican candidate win. What's been left is a mess here for Montana Democrats. The head of the state party just resigned and endorsed Bodnar. The Republican candidate is so confident in his win that he hasn't been coming to debates or even hosting many public events.

segments.speaker: Heather Tal Murphy
segments.text: I went to the godfather of Democratic politics in the state, Jon Tester, to see what he made of all this. Tester is the last Democrat elected to Senate in Montana, a seat he held for 18 years. He understands well how thin the margins can be in this red state. He once won his seat by fewer than 4,000 votes.

segments.speaker: Heather Tal Murphy
segments.text: Tester was one of the first big-name Democrats to support Bodnar. I heard many rumors that he was actually behind the scheme to pump money into the primary for Alani. But he insisted to me that he had nothing to do with it and thought it was, quote, "stupid." Still, he's clearly frustrated by Alani's decision to stay in the race.

segments.speaker: Jon Tester
segments.text: I don't know what her motivation is for running, but either way, I don't think there's an understanding of the gravity of the situation. I don't think there's an understanding of what's at risk here.

segments.speaker: Jon Tester
segments.text: Look, our democracy is hanging on by its fingernails, if that. Congress has been AWOL for a year and 3/4, and so is this important? Yeah, I mean, I'm 70 years old. I worked my whole damn life to make sure we have a country that my kids can enjoy and be able to prosper in-- my grandkids, too. That may be gone.

segments.speaker: Jon Tester
segments.text: And I've ran four times. And I can tell you when I was behind. And I can tell you when I was close to being ahead. And there's no way that anybody that knows anything about politics would say, if you're in Alani Bankhead's shoes, that I've got grassroots support and I'm going to win this thing. You're smoking something illegal, if that's what you're thinking. Because it ain't there. I don't see it. I have not seen it.

segments.speaker: Jon Tester
segments.text: There was a homecoming parade at the University of Montana that I was at this weekend. Bodnar had 40 people in his float. I saw one lady carrying an Alani Bankhead sign. If that's grassroots support that's going to push you across the finish line, you got a different view of politics in Montana than I do.

segments.speaker: Heather Tal Murphy
segments.text: I wanted to know what Alani made of that in these final days. I called her while she was on her way to a campaign event in Billings and played her what Tester said.

segments.speaker: Alani Bankhead
segments.text: I don't really care. I think Jon is pitching some kind of hissy fit. I put my ring in the hat. I won 48,000 votes. And if they want to support democracy, then they can support the Democratic candidate.

segments.speaker: Heather Tal Murphy
segments.text: I think Alani has truly convinced herself that it doesn't matter what the intention of the money was. She won the primary because voters, after learning about her, voted for her. There was this moment when I was watching her campaign at a fall festival in a small town outside of Helena. She made her way through the crowd and person after person stopped her, saying, hey, Alani, you got this, Alani. Nice to see you, Alani.

segments.speaker: Heather Tal Murphy
segments.text: They shake her hand, tap her on the shoulder. She seems to be enjoying herself. In all those other states, the Democratic candidate got out of the way for the independent. The one in South Dakota dropped out after his house caught on fire. Alani is the last one standing.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Heather Tal Murphy. Her story was produced by Miki Meek. Coming up, an oracle and a reporter walk into a bar-- ber shop. That's in a minute from Chicago Public Radio when our program continues.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: It's This American Life. I'm Ira Glass. Today's show-- Talk Me Into It. With the midterm elections upon us, we have stories of people convincing other people to change their minds. We've arrived at Act 2 of our program. For this act, we're going to leave the world of politics for just a minute and talk about the tactics of persuasion that professional salespeople use to get us to buy a car or a refrigerator or a timeshare or whatever. So this is Act 2, The Ben Franklin Close.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Noah Adams died a few weeks ago. And maybe you know who this is. He was one of the longtime hosts of All Things Considered on NPR. Back when I was young, I was his tape cutter for a while. And I have to say, I learned so much about interviewing listening to how he would structure his interviews and how he would come up with questions that drove in surprising directions. And since he died a couple of weeks ago, I've been thinking about one of the stories that he did that has always stuck with me.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And it was this story where he was not the interviewer. He was actually the interviewee in this story. And this was about one of the jobs that he did before he came to NPR. Noah had been a car salesman in Lexington, Kentucky at a VW dealership. And he was interviewed for this documentary called The Selling Game. And you'll hear, like, he's being interviewed. But mostly he just kind of tells this long story without a lot of interruption.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And in it, he explains that he used to go to these salesmen training seminars where they would teach different moves and sales techniques. And there was one technique that he saw people do and that he heard recordings of that he said, was just incredible, but he could never bring himself to do it. He said he would just be too embarrassed. As you'll hear, it requires a lot of shamelessness.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: The technique was called the Ben Franklin close. And Noah said that you would use this when you got the customer to the point where they had picked out the car, the insurance policy, or whatever it is you were selling. They had picked out the one they liked, but they just hadn't committed. They were hesitating. And then it's your job as a salesman to get them to buy right now. Like, don't wait, buy it right now.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And they're saying, I don't want to jump into it. I want to think about it. That's when it's time to kick in the Ben Franklin close.

segments.speaker: Noah Adams
segments.text: And you say, fine--

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: This is Noah.

segments.speaker: Noah Adams
segments.text: Let's think about it together. And you absolutely have to say, do you know who Ben Franklin was? You say this to a college professor. I mean, you have to say it. Do you know who Ben Franklin was? The reason you have to do it is because you get them involved and interacting with you.

segments.speaker: Noah Adams
segments.text: Yeah. We know who Ben Franklin was. Do you know what old Ben Franklin would do when he found himself in a situation like this? Then you'd wait, and they'd say-- they have to-- they have to say no, what would Ben Franklin do? At this point, you pull out a piece of paper, and a pencil, and ruler. It's a white piece of paper. Nothing on it.

segments.speaker: Noah Adams
segments.text: You say Ben Franklin, when he found himself in a situation just like this, couldn't decide what to do but take a piece of paper. And then you take the piece of paper out. And he'd draw a line down the middle. You draw a line. And he would then put on one side of that line the reasons why he should do this.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And then Noah explains that you, the salesman, then write down on the left side of the paper all the reasons why they should buy today. Our old car is on its last legs, and there's a special deal on financing. Like, whatever. Let's say there's a married couple there. You have them name reasons, and you name reasons. And then you write in big block letters. So you have to turn over the page and continue the list all the way down the back.

segments.speaker: Noah Adams
segments.text: Whatever product it is, if the salesman is any good at all, he can come up with about 20 reasons with the help of the customer why this should be done-- today, right now. And then-- and this is the fun part of it-- well then, what old Ben Franklin would do is take the other side of the page and write down the reasons why he shouldn't do this at this time.

segments.speaker: Noah Adams
segments.text: And then the salesman who has helped them, who has written down, in fact, in big block letters the reasons why they should, then takes the piece of paper very casually and pushes it across the desk and gives it to them, and gives them the pen and says, OK, very nicely. Now you folks write down the reasons why you shouldn't and just leans back. And he's not helping them at this point. And they're lost. They don't know what to do.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: I'm just going to jump in again. I think this moment is the reason that this stuck with me all these years, is that the whole sale is built around creating this very awkward social experience where you put the customers on the spot, and they find themselves suddenly participating in this really ridiculous exercise that you roped them into. And in theory, they could stand up and walk out, but doing that would just feel weird.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: It would be like violating some sort of social rules of sitting there in the room with you. And so these poor customers, they always play along. And they kind of tentatively pick up the pen like they've been instructed.

segments.speaker: Noah Adams
segments.text: And they look at each other. Well, let's see. Bob, what should we write? Let's put down this. Shouldn't jump into a decision. Number two, maybe it's too much money. And the salesman just sitting there waiting, and they look at him for help because he helped them with the other one. And he can't think of any reasons why they shouldn't buy it right now. And he just looks at them, and he's sort of tapping his finger on the desk. And time's going on, and the clock's ticking. And they get to three, maybe four.

segments.speaker: Noah Adams
segments.text: I've seen four. And then the salesman says, well, is that it? Is that all? And he says, let's see how many you got. Let's see. There's one, two, three, four, five, six-- 23 reasons why you should buy it today. And let me see how many you have. Here it says four. This is what Ben Franklin would do. He would then total up the reasons for and the reasons against.

segments.speaker: Noah Adams
segments.text: Then you just lay the paper on the table and sit there. And you sit there and sit there and sit there until they say something. And salesmen have a hard time doing this. You have to be quiet because the next move is theirs. They have to make it, and you should be willing to sit there and wait 30 minutes for them to do it.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: So you wait, Noah explains. He said what sometimes happens is that at this point, the customers will say what's really bothering them, like, why they are not buying right now. But Noah says any specific reason they give like the payments or whatever, any specific reason, a good salesman has an answer to that specific reason and can solve that problem for them and then close the sale.

segments.speaker: Noah Adams
segments.text: Is it the color? Is it me? Is it my company? Is it the delivery time? Is it the price? Can I give you more money? Can I get you a new one, you know, from the factory? I can get you this right now. You've got to get that objection. Turn it around. Use it to close.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: So it's pretty airtight. And the interviewer asks Noah, what can the consumer possibly say to get out of this and not buy this item?

segments.speaker: Noah Adams
segments.text: I thought of that many times. And when I used to go to these sales training seminars and listen to these people who are really good, I tried to figure out a way that a customer could get out of it. And there is only one way. And I figured it out, and I've used it a couple of times, and it's hard to do.

segments.speaker: Noah Adams
segments.text: The only way out is to be willing to step out of the role that you've created for yourself and say, I don't know why, I just don't want it. The salesman's been trained to handle every possible objection that you can come up with. There is not an objection you can come up with that the salesman has not been trained to take, turn completely around into a closing device, and pin you down to a contract.

segments.speaker: Noah Adams
segments.text: And if you say, I don't know why, I just don't want it-- I don't know why-- it'll floor him. He has no response to that.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Noah Adams in 1976 on a show called The Selling Game being interviewed by another old mentor of mine, Keith Talbot, who I am 100% sure is listening. Hello there, Keith. If you know Noah's work at all, you can totally understand why he would never be able to bring himself to do the Ben Franklin close. Noah was, like, the master of connecting with people, with anybody and getting them to open up.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: This kind of manipulation, just not his nature. Then Noah's wife, Neenah, says that she did see Noah tell salesmen a bunch of times, I don't know why. I just don't want it and then walk away. She says he got her doing it, too.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: All right, back to politics. Act 3, Polls, Schmolls. We now turn to one last persuader in this program of persuaders. This is a Republican in Pennsylvania. Seems to have a real gift for bringing voters over to his side. He also has some predictions and some thoughts about the polls that he was happy to share with our producer, Ike Sriskandarajah.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: Sam Negron is the Oracle of Allentown. I first met him two years ago at this weird moment in time. Remember when a comedian at a Trump rally called Puerto Rico an island of garbage? Sam was out here doing damage control with voters.

segments.speaker: Sam Negron
segments.text: There's 29 dump sites.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: He said it wasn't going to be a problem for Trump. And he was right. Trump did better with Hispanic voters than any Republican ever and picked up lots right here in Allentown. That's the Oracle. This time around, every poll is saying Hispanic support of Trump is down. But Sam's been knocking on thousands of doors for a PAC called Pennsylvania Republicanos. And again, he's saying it's not going to be a problem.

segments.speaker: Sam Negron
segments.text: And, I don't know where they're getting those numbers because it's not what I see. It's not what I find. And when I talk to people, what I find is that they're still on board, that they're still voting Republican, that they see the Democratic Party have been taken over by socialists. I've even been able to help a few switch parties through our slate cards that have--

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: From Democrat to Republican-- registered Republican in the last year?

segments.speaker: Sam Negron
segments.text: Yeah. The last two months, I've flipped a couple of people. They were frustrated with the Democrats, and I'm like, well, come here, I got you.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: What's going on? What--

segments.speaker: Sam Negron
segments.text: I'm telling you, Ike.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: So, that's the mission. Is Sam right? We head out onto the streets of this majority-Hispanic town to find out if Trump voters really are sticking with Republicans. It's slow going at first finding voters until we stopped by a barber shop.

segments.speaker: Sam Negron
segments.text: This is my favorite part of town because it's still affordable, and it's not so much drama.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: There's a reason why barber shops are a cliche of election coverage. It's a room designed for long conversations, and Sam happens to know the barber here from way back. He actually wanted his sister to date him, but she thought he was too nice. Sam hasn't seen him in more than a decade.

segments.speaker: Sam Negron
segments.text: We'll see if Willie's here. I won't even know if I'll recognize him. He was a pretty kid. Willie?

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: He's right there with the red hat.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: Willie Castillo is happy to see Sam. He tells him he's got six kids now. Sam says I've got five. Raised five more. Willie's like, hey, do you remember my brother? He's cutting hair just over there. Sam's like, remember my sister? She's still crazy.

segments.speaker: Sam Negron
segments.text: I used to be on her, like, yo, Willie's a good kid. He's too nice.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: Then Sam tells him why he's here.

segments.speaker: Sam Negron
segments.text: In 2019, I switched parties to Republican.

segments.speaker: Willie Castillo
segments.text: Yeah, right?

segments.speaker: Sam Negron
segments.text: And I've been somebody that some people see me as influential and helping other Hispanics what I consider see the light, right?

segments.speaker: Willie Castillo
segments.text: Right.

segments.speaker: Sam Negron
segments.text: And--

segments.speaker: Willie Castillo
segments.text: I am a Republican, bro, just so you know.

segments.speaker: Sam Negron
segments.text: OK. And that was the main question. There's news reports all over the place saying that a lot of Hispanics that swung towards the Republican Party and voted for Trump are two years later regretting doing that vote. And that's the question, right?

segments.speaker: Willie Castillo
segments.text: In the past two years, I haven't regretted that I supported him.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: Sam is looking at me smiling with his arms open, like, see, Willie is even on board with how Trump is removing immigrants.

segments.speaker: Willie Castillo
segments.text: I actually got, no lie, friends that I found out that they were illegal after they got arrested by ICE.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: In the last two years?

segments.speaker: Willie Castillo
segments.text: Yeah. Those people, they got taken by ICE and they got deported.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: These are good friends of yours?

segments.speaker: Willie Castillo
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: Even though your own friends have been removed from this country by the Trump administration, you still support the Republican party?

segments.speaker: Willie Castillo
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: Can you explain that? Because I think that might be a hard thing for people to understand.

segments.speaker: Willie Castillo
segments.text: I'll be honest with you. I know a lot of immigrants that came into this country, personally, that don't belong here not because they're immigrants, because they're criminals. They're criminals.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: Just for the record. The vast majority of immigrants detained and deported by the Trump administration have no criminal record.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: How about your friends? Had they been--

segments.speaker: Willie Castillo
segments.text: My friends are not criminals. The people I know, they're not criminals. They're good people. They wanted to come here and work. But, no. You came in a certain way. Now you got to go back.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: So Willie's still backing the president and his party. That's one point for Sam. Willie's 21-year-old son is quietly listening. He's cutting hair, too. I ask him where he's at, but he's like, nah, I didn't vote and is certain he will not be voting anytime soon. He sends me to AJ, another younger guy who's been listening nearby.

segments.speaker: Aj
segments.text: I voted Trump. Trump, yeah.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: How do you feel now?

segments.speaker: Aj
segments.text: Yeah, I'm not really into all of them-- everything he got going on. I just know a little bit here and there.

segments.speaker: Sam Negron
segments.text: Do you regret voting for him?

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: Sam jumps in.

segments.speaker: Sam Negron
segments.text: Do you feel like it might have been a mistake voting for him?

segments.speaker: Aj
segments.text: The regret is probably from the racistness. Like, people be saying he's racist, all that. But no, I don't. Me personally, I don't regret it. No. Yeah. He knows what he's doing most of the time.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: That's another point for Sam. In the waiting chairs at the front, I meet another guy, Black guy. Hang on-- honorary Dominican, according to a barber nearby. He's also sticking with Trump. He wishes ICE would go further. Not technically a Hispanic voter, but I'll give Sam the honorary point. Sam's killing it. His prophecies coming true.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: Outside, we run into one more person, Rolando Rolon, an older Puerto Rican guy who was sitting on a pink camp chair in front of the store. He's got a cane, aviators on, and lots of jewelry on his hands and neck. He's been voting Republican for a long time, and he also stands by his vote for Trump.

segments.speaker: Rolando Rolon
segments.text: Because that job is a tough job. And the mess that was happened before, it's not easy to fix it in two years.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: He's going to vote Republican in the midterms, but with one possible exception.

segments.speaker: Rolando Rolon
segments.text: I understand the government is Democrat, and I admit it. He's doing a good job.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: Which one?

segments.speaker: Rolando Rolon
segments.text: Shapiro.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: The governor. Yeah.

segments.speaker: Rolando Rolon
segments.text: I got to be realistic. He's doing a good job.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: You're going to vote for Shapiro for governor?

segments.speaker: Rolando Rolon
segments.text: I'm not sure.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: Sam senses opportunity like when a lion hears a gazelle step on a branch. His head snaps towards the undecided voter.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: [SPEAKING SPANISH]

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: Rolando also perks up. He obviously would rather talk to Sam than me. Sam asks him, what do you know about the Republican candidate for governor, Stacy Garrity?

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: [SPEAKING SPANISH]

segments.speaker: Sam Negron
segments.text: You speak English. I know Stacy. I can't say that I know her personally. I've done a lot of work with Stacy as--

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: Sam pulls up pictures on his phone. He's done private security at some Garrity events. And these are of him and Garrity, videos he's taken behind the scenes with her. Also pictures of her in uniform. He talks about her military service, her years in Harrisburg as treasurer.

segments.speaker: Sam Negron
segments.text: It's somebody that you really need to look into because Stacy Garrity--

segments.speaker: Sam Negron
segments.text: [SPEAKING SPANISH]

segments.speaker: Sam Negron
segments.text: --and look up on the information. She's the one running against Shapiro. They just had a debate. There was several times that the moderators had to say to him after he finished answering, OK, can you answer the question now.

segments.speaker: Sam Negron
segments.text: [LAUGHS]

segments.speaker: Sam Negron
segments.text: You know what I mean? So something that--

segments.speaker: Rolando Rolon
segments.text: You monkey around.

segments.speaker: Sam Negron
segments.text: Right. You know attorneys, brother. They're good at talking and saying stuff. For me, it's different, especially with her, since I've done protection for her so many times. It's different when you go to a place and you see these candidates talk. Obviously, they got their game face on. It's different when we're in a back room waiting, and I'm helping her mom get into a chair, and we're talking. I find her to be a very genuine person, someone who really cares. And I believe that she would be the better candidate.

segments.speaker: Sam Negron
segments.text: That's just my opinion. But it's something you should look into.

segments.speaker: Rolando Rolon
segments.text: Yeah I think--

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: What's he going to say faced with that charismatic sell?

segments.speaker: Rolando Rolon
segments.text: To be honest with you, I'm not going to vote for Josh Shapiro after what he told me.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: Somehow millions of dollars in Stacy Garrity ads hadn't reached him. But Sam did. That's one last bonus point for Sam.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: That was crazy.

segments.speaker: Sam Negron
segments.text: Right.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: Did you bring me to Republican headquarters disguised as a barber shop?

segments.speaker: Sam Negron
segments.text: No, brother. What I'm finding is that most of us are still on board. I was a little worried at first, but now I'm not worried. I think we got this.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: A lot of people are predicting a blue wave.

segments.speaker: Sam Negron
segments.text: For real?

segments.speaker: Sam Negron
segments.text: [LAUGHS]

segments.speaker: Sam Negron
segments.text: I never heard that. I can show you my Facebook. It's all red, brother. From all the people that I've spoken to, I don't see a blue wave coming. I don't see it. It would shock the hell out of me.

segments.speaker: Ike Sriskandarajah
segments.text: I called the Oracle back just days before the election. He's still predicting a red wave, with a Republican winning his local congressional district and Republicans gaining seats in the House and the Senate. For Pennsylvania Governor, he says Stacy Garrity will beat Josh Shapiro. All of these predictions are the opposite of what the polls say. On Tuesday, we get to find out if Sam is still the Oracle of Allentown.
